pages.text: Four thousand years ago, in the land of Egypt, there lived a poor man named Khun-Anup. His home was an oasis in the desert, west of the River Nile. One day his family’s grain was almost finished. He loaded his donkeys with the goods of the oasis: salt, reeds, herbs, and the skins of wild animals. “I am going down to the city to trade these for grain,” he told his wife. He walked for many days. At last he came to a narrow path between the river and a field of barley.
sentences: Four thousand years ago, in the land of Egypt, there lived a poor man named Khun-Anup.
His home was an oasis in the desert, west of the River Nile.
One day his family’s grain was almost finished.
He loaded his donkeys with the goods of the oasis: salt, reeds, herbs, and the skins of wild animals.
“I am going down to the city to trade these for grain,” he told his wife.
He walked for many days.
At last he came to a narrow path between the river and a field of barley.
pages.alt: A thin peasant in a linen kilt leading loaded donkeys along a path beside the Nile.

pages.text: The land there was farmed by a man named Nemtynakht. He saw the loaded donkeys, and he wanted them. So he spread a sheet of cloth across the path, with one edge in the water and the other in the barley. “Take care, peasant,” he called. “Do not tread on my cloth.” Khun-Anup could not go through the river. He led his donkeys along the edge of the field. One donkey bit off a mouthful of barley. “Thief!” shouted Nemtynakht. “Your donkey has eaten my grain. I shall take them all.” And he beat the peasant with his stick.

“Take care, peasant,” he called.
“Do not tread on my cloth.” Khun-Anup could not go through the river.
He led his donkeys along the edge of the field.
One donkey bit off a mouthful of barley.
“Thief!” shouted Nemtynakht.
“Your donkey has eaten my grain.
I shall take them all.” And he beat the peasant with his stick.
pages.alt: A cloth stretched across a narrow path between a river and a barley field, with a stout man blocking the way.

pages.text: Khun-Anup wept for his donkeys, but nobody came to help. For ten days he begged Nemtynakht, who only laughed. Then the peasant walked to the city and found the High Steward, Rensi, who was Nemtynakht’s master and a judge. Khun-Anup had no money and no friends. He had only his tongue. He bowed and began to speak. “High Steward, you are the father of the orphan and the husband of the widow. You are the steering oar of the whole land. Do justice, for justice lasts for ever.” Rensi had never heard a poor man speak so well.

He bowed and began to speak.
“High Steward, you are the father of the orphan and the husband of the widow.
You are the steering oar of the whole land.
Do justice, for justice lasts for ever.” Rensi had never heard a poor man speak so well.
pages.alt: A peasant bowing and speaking with one hand raised before a high official seated on a chair.

pages.text: Rensi went to the King. “My lord, I have found a peasant who speaks most beautifully. He has been robbed.” The King loved fine words. “Do not answer him yet,” he said. “Let him keep speaking, and have every word written down and brought to me. But see that his wife and children are sent food each day, and feed him too, without his knowing who sends it.” So Rensi said nothing. Khun-Anup came back the next day and spoke again. And the next. Scribes sat behind a screen and wrote down every word.

He has been robbed.” The King loved fine words.
“Do not answer him yet,” he said.
“Let him keep speaking, and have every word written down and brought to me.
But see that his wife and children are sent food each day, and feed him too, without his knowing who sends it.” So Rensi said nothing.
Khun-Anup came back the next day and spoke again.
And the next.
Scribes sat behind a screen and wrote down every word.
pages.alt: A scribe seated cross-legged behind a screen, writing on a long scroll, while a peasant speaks beyond it.

pages.text: Nine times Khun-Anup came. At first he praised the High Steward. When no answer came, he grew bolder. “You were set here to stop the robber, and you have become his shelter. The scales must not tilt. The one who should punish wrong is doing wrong himself.” Rensi’s guards beat him for his boldness, and still he spoke. After the ninth speech, he had no hope left. “I have begged, and you have not heard,” he said. “Now I shall go and complain of you to the god of the dead.” He turned to leave.

“You were set here to stop the robber, and you have become his shelter.
The scales must not tilt.
The one who should punish wrong is doing wrong himself.” Rensi’s guards beat him for his boldness, and still he spoke.
After the ninth speech, he had no hope left.
“I have begged, and you have not heard,” he said.
“Now I shall go and complain of you to the god of the dead.” He turned to leave.
pages.alt: A peasant standing straight and speaking boldly while guards with sticks stand at either side.

pages.text: “Stay,” said Rensi. He had the scrolls brought out and read aloud, all nine speeches. Khun-Anup listened in wonder. Then the scrolls were sent to the King, who was more pleased with them than with anything in his kingdom. “Judge the case yourself,” he told Rensi. Rensi did. Nemtynakht was brought in, and everything he owned, his house, his fields, and his cattle, was given to the peasant. The donkeys were given back as well. The story was copied by Egyptian scribes for centuries. It is one of the oldest stories in the world about a poor person who spoke up and won.

activities.question: How did Nemtynakht trap the peasant?
options: He dug a pit in the path
He spread a cloth across the path so the donkeys had to walk beside his barley
He hid the peasant’s donkeys at night

activities.question: What was the only thing Khun-Anup had to fight with?
Why did the King order that the peasant should not be answered at once?
options: He wanted to hear more of his fine speeches and have them written down

activities.question: Apply it: A market woman is cheated by a powerful person and has no money for a lawyer. Using the tale, what can she still do?
options: Speak up clearly and persistently to those who can give justice

activities.prompt: Put the events of the story in order.
items: Khun-Anup sets out with his donkeys to buy grain
Nemtynakht takes the donkeys and beats him
Khun-Anup speaks before the High Steward
The King has his speeches written down
Nemtynakht’s property is given to the peasant

activities.definition: Fair treatment according to what is right.
